segments.text: This is an ABC podcast.
Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report. I'm Norman Swan.
Today, developer of the human papillomavirus vaccine, Professor Ian Fraser, on the prospects for a coronavirus vaccine.
And the growing debate about how we get out of this. What's the off-ramp and what's at the end of that slip road?
Is it life as we knew it, BC, before coronavirus?
virus and is elimination of the virus from Australia not just feasible, but in fact the
only sensible option. The clamour from Australian business is growing, the backroom lobbying
intensifying. The numbers of new cases are small, people are saying, so let's take the
food off the break now and get the economy back on its feet and people back to work.
Last week, the federal government under pressure released the modelling on which they relied
for their early decision making and implied that their future decisions on controls would
also be guided by modelling. So what are we facing and does modelling help? Well the first thing to
state and most governments are stating it clearly, the economy won't be fixed until you've fixed the
pandemic. And Australia has a better chance than most because our borders are closed and will be
for a long time to come. And we have as a community socially distanced with wider criteria for testing
and more effective contact tracing, isolation and quarantine. But under the surface we have local
spread in the community that's either steady or is in Tasmania spiking. And remember 50% of the
spread of COVID-19 virus comes from asymptomatic people and without social distancing and other
controls each person passes it on to nearly three other people. So if we're seeing say 50 new cases
a day and we lift the lid on social distancing the most effect that's the most effective
of containment measure we have, then 50 can become a very large number of new cases each day all too
quickly. Remember, there was a time, sometime in December, I should say, when Wuhan had only one
person with what would come to be known as COVID-19. Only one person. And we're now at well
over 1.8 million cases with more than 100,000 deaths globally in just four and a half horrific
months. In Australia, we have the luxury of a debate about what comes next. Do we keep up the
rhetoric of flattening the curve, which means squishing the epidemic out for months? Or do we
do what the New Zealanders have aimed for, which is elimination of spread altogether, or as close
as you can get to that? Michael Baker is Professor of Public Health at the University of Otago in
Wellington and sits on New Zealand's National Technical Committee advising on their response.
Like most countries, we were pursuing the standard pandemic model in response to COVID-19.
And of course, that's written for influenza.
And it did start to dawn on quite a few of us that maybe we should look or learn more from the experience in China
and what the Chinese had done to halt a pandemic really in full flight.
And other Asian countries were pursuing a similar approach, particularly South Korea and Hong Kong and Taiwan.
So we really advocated very strongly in New Zealand
that we should look at containing this infection.
And also, I think probably like Australia,
we had a little bit more breathing space.
New Zealand then really, I think, had that choice.
I mean, we were heading down a mitigation path,
trying to flatten the curve.
But then we suggested to the government,
and I'm on the technical advisory group for the response,
that an elimination strategy could work.
And there was obviously quite a bit of internal discussion,
but eventually we switched tacks.
So you switched tax from essentially flattening the curve and making sure you didn't get a horrible peak with lots of people dying to saying, well, maybe we could bottom this one out.
Well, actually, we could actually eliminate the virus entirely from New Zealand.
And there was a lot of doubt from many of my colleagues that that was going to be possible.
But we were tracking down the standard influenza model, which I think the pandemic plan is written for.
but we felt actually this was more like a SARS virus
and that basically containment with the goal of elimination was actually viable.
So just as in 2002-2003 SARS disappeared,
this is what you think you could do with closed borders with SARS-CoV-2?
That's right.
Even though obviously it's very infectious, which made it difficult,
because it had the longer incubation period,
which was more typical of a SARS virus or other coronaviruses,
more like five or six days, compared with influenza,
which is one to three days, it meant that those containment measures, stamping it out,
so that's case identification, isolation, contact tracing, quarantine, they can work if they're done very rigorously.
But the difficulty is when you're in this intense response mode, it's very hard to change your direction
and our politicians weren't initially convinced, but they came round.

But the difficulty was that we just didn't have the infrastructure ready to manage a containment process very well because the public health system in New Zealand has been wound down, as it has, I think, in a number of countries.
So it was completely in reactive mode.
We didn't have large numbers of staff to do the contact tracing.
And our borders were still a bit porous.
We were relying on a fairly soft form of self-isolation, home quarantine.
So a lot of things had to happen very quickly.
and it became fairly obvious that we needed a complete rapid shutdown of the country
just to give us time to get these systems operating
and also to extinguish some of the chains of virus transmission.
So Jacinta Darin announced a strict lockdown.
When was that again?
Well, it was basically announced on the 23rd of March
and it came into effect on the 26th of March.
So we're now a bit over two weeks into it.
And you're using this time to ramp up your testing infrastructure
and your contact tracing infrastructure.
That's right.
And of course, we went into a full supervised border quarantine system about a week ago.
So what are you driving for?
You're driving for zero spread in New Zealand.
That's right.
And since the lockdown started two weeks ago, we've seen the numbers track down.
I mean, it is a very effective way of dampening down transmission.
Do you have modelling or anything that tells you when you might hit the deck here?
What's the prediction about when New Zealand might actually get to zero transmission?
Well, there's one model and it's still being reviewed reactively.
And it says that after four weeks of lockdown, we might just be there.
So give or take end of April, beginning of May.
That's right.
And how many new cases a day were you having before the Prime Minister announced the lockdown and the border controls?
We're having about 90 cases a day.
And yesterday we had 18 cases.
So it's been tracking down now for about a week.
So in other words, we can't use the excuse in Australia that you're smaller than us because we've got about 100 cases a day and the community transmission is about 50 or so.
So it's very similar numbers when you started.
Yeah.
So what does the off-ramp look like?
Let's say you get down to zero spread beginning of May.
What happens next, which is the question that everybody's asking around the world, particularly in Australia, but I'm sure you are in New Zealand.
Yeah, I agree.
That's a huge issue.
And it's not going from lockdown.
There's no question that we're going to remove everything.
It would be gradually ramping things down.
There's a whole lot of things that obviously have to be working very well.
We have to be very confident in the border quarantine,
the ability to rapidly identify cases and stamp them out,
and also thinking about all the backstop surveillance systems that have to be operating,
so lots of testing and starting to test in other settings.
We're thinking about other things like testing sewage, for instance,
for traces of the virus.
That's far more speculative.
The other thing is all these other surveillance systems
that are giving us an idea of how the population behaviour has changed.
So we're using telecom data and Google mobility data
and all of that's pointing in the right direction.
But what gets allowed first?
Have you modelled that? Have you thought about it?
The opportunities to de-escalate the levels
is particularly more people going back to work
and schools are likely to open actually at the end of this month
on a limited basis. And then you just watch and see what happens? Yes, watching very carefully.
And this huge public support in New Zealand, and I think the thing that happened here was the
government took a very decisive approach. And basically, everything in New Zealand was shut
down unless it was an essential industry. And the public was informed they could only travel for
very limited reasons, for very short distances, just the nearest place they could get food,
and for medical care. The government did take on the message that you're doing things almost
in a reverse way from what you normally do in a pandemic response. With an elimination approach,
you have to basically almost reverse the normal pandemic response because with influenza,
and it's really kind of built into the planning, you gradually ramp up the response as the pandemic
gets more intense and you hold and reserve the more difficult or disruptive measures like shutting
schools and so on to a later stage maybe to take the edge off the peak whereas with an elimination
approach you do things almost in reverse as soon as you get any evidence of local transmission
you throw everything at it to suppress the transmission while you've got all your other
systems while you're getting them all working properly and that's really what New Zealand's
done. Michael Becker is Professor of Public Health at the University of Otago in Wellington.
You're listening to RN's Health Report with me, Norman Swan.
So let's get down to this debate about whether we should target elimination of spread in Australia.
The modelling released by the government last week doesn't help much,
apart from reminding us how bad COVID-19 could be.
Professor Jodie McVernon led the modelling exercise for the government at the Doherty Institute in Melbourne.
What we were trying to achieve with this modelling was to give our government
some perspective on what this epidemic might look like without control,
and then to think about how we could use the various public health measures available to us
in the absence of definitive treatments or vaccines to reduce its impact.
And the models that we had developed in the preparedness phase were expressly focused on the impact on the healthcare system
and being able to ensure that we would have sufficient capacity in the healthcare system to manage cases,
particularly severe cases, was a real priority.
All of us as modelers were putting scenarios to our governments, those of us who were working with policy,
that were jaw-dropping. It was very hard to countenance this threat. You know, I think all
of us saw the lockdown in Wuhan and thought, well, obviously we could never do that here.
And then in a very short space of time, we realised this was part of the toolkit.
You know, we'd had a discussion about what social distancing would look like in Australia,
and most pandemic plans talked about things like school closure or, you know, less intrusive
measures, but talked about how economically costly those measures were. And suddenly we were in a
a ballpark that was completely different.
The problem was clearly one nobody wanted to have,
but the solutions really became universally clear
that this needed a really combined suite of interventions.
Was there a light bulb moment for you
where you were really shocked?
Most of us in the modelling community
were really, really worried early on.
And I think one of the things that worried us
was the public complacency in many situations.
And we've seen that spill out in policy
in other parts of the world.
I think when something is so bad and so hard to believe,
It's easier to wish it away.
But seeing then the further epidemics rolling out in other parts of the world
made it absolutely clear that this was not a bad dream.
Professor Geordie McVernon of the Doherty Institute.
It's important to appreciate that our pandemic planning, like New Zealand's,
had been based on influenza,
which helps to explain the slow ramp up of control measures
rather than going hard early.
For a while, the government appeared to be stuck in the flu mode of thinking.
But the COVID-19 virus isn't the flu.

It's a SARS-like virus and needs tough, prolonged action with the tantalising prospect, perhaps like SARS, of elimination of spread within our borders, assuming our borders stay closed for many months.
The difference, though, with SARS-CoV-2 is that it spreads from asymptomatic people who can be hard to find.
Associate Professor Kamalini-Lokogi is in the Research School of Public Health at the Australian National University.
There's probably no Australian public health researcher
with the range and depth of on-the-ground experience of controlling outbreaks
and the health consequences of humanitarian crises.
For example, she was heavily involved with Ebola control in Africa.
Kamalini Lukoge is a strong proponent, when there's no vaccine, no treatment,
and a non-immune population, of aiming for elimination of spread,
having seen it work on the ground.
And also argues that modelling won't help you much in getting there.
What's required is traditional epidemic control.
What we need to look at, Norman, for achieving elimination and staying there is particularly how do we make sure we're finding out about community transmission of COVID-19.

So the way we do that is to expand our testing capacity, to do very effective thorough contact tracing, so following up of those who may have been in contact, and quarantining and effectively managing those contacts.
Modelling is part of that process of knowing how many we might need to look at,
where we need to look.
But really the key to controlling the disease is the public health response.
And by the public health response, I also mean the public's response.
And the Australian community has, through taking on these very strong measures,
bought us, the public health expert community, time for us to put in place those measures.

And we need to recognise the value of that gift they've given us and really work hard to make sure that we have the systems in place that allow us to know we've eliminated disease and then make sure we know once we start lifting containment measures that we're still on top of it.
Associate Professor Kamalini-Lokoghe.
Having said that modelling has limited value in working towards elimination,
a group at the University of Sydney has indeed modelled how we get to elimination of spread in Australia.
And social distancing is the core strategy.
Professor Mikhail Prokopenko is director of the Centre for Complex Systems at Sydney University.
We try to focus on modelling COVID at the scale of all of Australia, but using an individual-based approach.

So essentially, we have in a digital form 24 million agents, each of which represents anonymously a single individual and distributions of households, household compositions, places of work and schools to a large level of detail.

Then, once the pandemic starts, we try to model every single day by estimating interactions within different social contexts, households, neighbours, communities, working groups, schools, different grades and so on.
Then we can estimate the dynamics in terms of the newly daily cases and correlate it with the actual timelines.
And what do you find when you plug in, say, social distancing and effectiveness of current policies?
So this model allows us to specifically evaluate different degrees of compliance with social distancing and different degrees of compliance with case isolation.
We focused on comparing compliance with social distancing between, say, 70 percent, 80 percent, 90 percent of the population following these rules.
And one interesting result was that there is a sharp divide, a transition between 70% compliance and 80%.
So if we as population follow the 80% or better 90% compliance, we could hope to get the numbers of cases down by July to pretty much near zero territory.
However, if we relax it and stay on a 70% trajectory, numbers don't even go down.
They keep rising even after some inflection point.
What it means is that we can't really relax what we have been doing so far in the near future.
So the model shows that we are pretty much at the peak, not only at the incidence peak, the new cases,
But we are pretty much, as we speak, are sitting on the prevalence peak.
So the active cases are probably reducing.
So if we are continuing on this path, we are quite likely to get to a really controlled situation by July.
If we relax it, the curves will start shooting up.
One of the arguments is that you could mitigate that by a very wide testing regimen, more effective isolation and quarantining and contact tracing.
I understand that it is a necessary part, but it would not be sufficient if we only stay with case isolation and home quarantine and tracing immediate contacts.
And the reason is that there are those asymptomatic cases which do have probability of passing this infection in a stealthy, silent way.
If we just reduce our intervention to pure mitigation, like what you just said, that would not be sufficient.
Because you have to realize, I mean, if I use this analogy of any football game,
we started this game against an opponent which overplayed us
and we were conceding goals left and right.
And now we're getting to a halftime and we're almost equalized.
But should we start the second half and again relax,
we will be at best just maintaining a draw.
We'll end up in extra time and who wants to be in extra time?
So what I'm saying is we have to be vigilant.
we have to go on offensive and that means we have to be aggressively stopping these social
interactions and maintaining social distancing then by the end of maybe june by early july
we should be in a winning position what does winning look like when the virus is still around
that's also a very good question because we are in a preferential position here
being isolated naturally geographically from land traffic.
And if we maintain these international travel restrictions on air,
we should be able to get back our economy to some decent level,
maybe not 100% level, but to some decent level,
and maintain that for as long as needed to get efficient vaccine available.
Our model showed that even a three-day delay in introducing tough social distancing measures
means that three weeks need to be added at the end of the suppression period.
So essentially have a week for a day, approximately.
So just to clarify that, what you're seeing is for every three days delay in getting to lockdown,
you get three weeks extension to the epidemic at the other end.
That's right.
Basically, it's an approximate equation here, which came out of the model.
We didn't put it in.
for one extra day of a delay, you get one extra week at the end of the epidemic that we need to
be in this social distancing, almost in lockdown. Just pursuing that for a moment though, our
community transmission levels are at low levels. Doesn't that make us like New Zealand, that we're
actually at low numbers and we've got the chance to turn it down quickly? Or is that just wishful
thinking on my part? It's a good situation to be in, but you could still multiply these numbers
to a sufficient level. You know, in modeling, there is this old saying that all models are wrong,
but some are more useful than others. For example, in the model I was describing,
the one which we've done in the Union of Sydney, there is a clear divide between 70% compliance
and 80% compliance. It's a transition. So when you have those sharp divisions, it means you found a
gem which clearly could be used in decision making and that is something which could be
immediately actioned by the society. One message here is that it's not just reliance on the
government, it's our own social behaviour that has to change and change to some extent which will get
us out of it. Professor Mikhail Prokopenko is Director of the Centre for Complex Systems
at the University of Sydney. So everyone's hanging out for a vaccine and lots of research groups
around the world are having a go.
The Australian with the most success in vaccine development
is Professor Ian Fraser.
The virus was the human papillomavirus,
which causes cervical cancer,
and the immunisation took years of work.
Ian is still active in vaccine development.
Ian, welcome back to The Health Report.
Norman, it's good to speak with you.
What's the challenge here?
The challenge is the coronavirus, let's face it.
We have a lot of people who are working to develop vaccines
against this particular coronavirus.
But we haven't had much success with coronavirus vaccines in the past.
And that's partly because it seems to be a difficult virus
to get a successful and safe vaccine against,
and partly because the virus infects a bit of us,
which our immune system doesn't really do very well at protecting.
Meaning the upper respiratory tract, the nose and throat?
Indeed, indeed.
I mean, it's a separate immune system, if you like, of its own,
which isn't easily accessible by vaccine technology.
So just explain why not, because there's a blood supply,
we've got white blood cells.
Why is there this problem with the upper respiratory tract?
And it's true of influenza as well.
We've got a pretty lousy vaccine to influenza.
It's the best we've got.
We want to get a vaccine that stops the cells getting infected.
And that really means that you've got to have something
that can neutralise the virus outside of the body
because effectively our upper airway is outside of the body.
This is mind-bending, but really it feels as if it's inside,
but in fact it's an external surface,
even though it might be surrounded by your nose and throat.
Yeah, it's a bit like your skin.
It's trying to get a vaccine to kill a virus on the surface of your skin.
We do have, of course, the ability to put some antibody in there
and that we have a local immune system in our lungs
which makes the right sort of antibody,
but that doesn't connect quite as well as it should do
with the systemic immune system that would respond to a vaccine.
And one of the problems with corona vaccines in the past
has been that when that immune response does cross across
to where the virus infected cells are,
it actually increases the pathology rather than reducing it
so that immunisation with SARS corona vaccine
caused in animals inflammation in the lungs
which wouldn't otherwise have been there
if the vaccine hadn't been given.
Because you're trying to get the virus once it's in.
Now, this virus mutates.
In fact, they're being able to track the vaccine through the world
and where it came from by its mutations.
Is the mutation rate changing its coat enough to confuse a vaccine?
I don't think so.
The total number of mutations to date has been quite small.
It seems to be very small point mutations in the genetic information.
and from what we've seen so far over the course of basically now four or five months of keeping
a track of this virus nothing has changed enough that it would prevent the immune system having a
go. We still have to identify what the best target in the virus is. It seems likely that it would be
some part of the spike protein which is the bit that allows the virus to stick to cells but there
hasn't been enough change there yet to prevent a vaccine that worked against the first version of
this virus, now coping with the minor changes that have occurred.
What's the story with antibodies to this coronavirus with SARS-CoV-2?
Every day goes by and you seem to get a different story.
Some people get a strong antibody response.
Some people get a weak antibody response.
There's a story of do people get reinfected?
How long does immunity last?
Have we got any visibility?
And that's critical to whether or not a vaccine is going to work, is it not?
Indeed.
And for data on that, we really have to go back to when people were doing research on the coronaviruses that caused the common cold.
And at that time, there was quite a lot of work done on how long antibody responses lasted after the infection.
And yes, you get antibody after natural infection.
Yes, it lasts for a while.
But it's not lifelong by any stretch of the imagination, sort of months rather than years.
And of course, we don't know what would happen with a vaccine in terms of longevity of immune response.
We've got to, first of all, find a vaccine that will work, and then we can see how long it's going to work for.
But I think it would be fair to say that the natural immunity that you get after infection for this coronavirus is probably going to turn out like the coronavirus, as we've seen in the past.
Yes, there will be some natural protection over a period of months, maybe even years, but it won't be lifelong.

On the other hand, the good news is that if you get reinfected with the virus a second time some months down the track, probably there will be enough immunity there to stop you becoming seriously ill.
Now, there's about 70 different technologies being deployed from using the virus like you would an influenza.
You'd kill it and try and put it in.
There's putting in little parcels of messenger RNA to tell the cell to produce antibodies.
Really clever stuff.
And, you know, the University of Queensland, they're clamping the molecule and trying to get an antibody response to that.
And they're trying to get very specific.
I mean, what I understand is there's a 90 percent attrition rate in vaccine development.
So 90% of these are likely to fail.
I mean, where's the smart money on the vaccine development at the moment?
Well, the smart money has to be on something which will produce a strong antibody response.
And the best way we know to do that is protein plus adjuvant.
And that would probably be my best.
So to translate that, that means a significant part of the virus attached to a chemical which induces an immune response.
That's exactly right.
and that has been successful in animal models for coronaviruses in the past
and that's of course where the money is being put I suspect in large measure at the moment.
I mean another sort of vaccine would be just antibody transferred from somebody who'd been
infected already and had got rid of the infection. It's not strictly a vaccine but it would be an
immunological means of preventing infection and that would probably be something that would be
more quickly developed than an actual vaccine. Now some people argue that that's a dirty vaccine
you've just described and that's why you got the problem with SARS in 2003 when they reinfected the
monkeys and they got this strong and nasty immune response and that why they're going for targeted
very specific antibody responses. Well that's probably correct if there is if we don't know
exactly which bit of the virus would best protect us if we got an immune response against it but
And even with the SARS vaccines, there was pulmonary immunopathology.
In other words, the lungs got inflamed after vaccination
with some of the virus-like particle-based vaccines
that were also tried for the SARS infection.
So it's not just dirty antibody.
If we pick the wrong antigen for a vaccine
where we're making a defined vaccine, a controlled vaccine,
if we pick the wrong antigen, we may get the same problem.
Ian Fraser, you're not painting an optimistic picture of a vaccine
in 12 to 18 months?
Well, the good news is that, as you've pointed out,
there are at least 80 known vaccine experiments going on at the moment,
including five that are in human trials,
so that we've got the best possible chance of getting something.
I guess the slightly less good news is that the reason we're doing
all these different methods is because there isn't an obvious winner.
And I think it would be fair to say that because of the safety issue,
and the safety issue is a real one,
And even if we get something which looks quite encouraging in animals,
the safety trials in humans will have to be fairly extensive
before we would think about vaccinating a group of people
who had not yet been exposed to the virus
and therefore might hope to get protection,
but certainly wouldn't be keen to accept a possibility
of really serious side effects if they actually caught the virus.
Ian Fraser, thanks for joining us.
Thank you, Norman.
Professor Ian Fraser is at the University of Queensland.
This has been The Health Report. I'm Norman Swan.
And don't forget Coronacast, which you can get from any of,
wherever you get your podcasts.
You've been listening to an ABC podcast.
Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives
on the ABC Listen app.
